analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring federal construction contractors to pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Education and the Workforce Committee after being referred there on February 13, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally funded construction projects — public buildings, highways, and other public works — to pay workers at least the locally prevailing wage for their trade. This bill would repeal that requirement entirely and erase any other law's references to it, taking effect 30 days after enactment while leaving existing contracts untouched [S2][S3]. In practice, that would let federal contractors pay whatever wage they could get away with on projects funded by taxpayers. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors holding or seeking federal contracts would benefit most, because they could lower their labor costs by paying below-prevailing wages. Contractors using nonunion labor, in particular, would no longer need to match the local union rate to win federal work.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, ending the requirement that federally financed or federally assisted construction pay the locally prevailing wage to laborers and mechanics [S2][S3].
It also voids any references in other laws to Davis-Bacon wage requirements after enactment, wiping out prevailing-wage rules embedded in other federal programs [S2][S3].
For contractors, the direct effect is the ability to bid federal work at lower labor cost, since prevailing-wage obligations frequently set pay at or near the local union scale.

analysis.who_pays: Workers on federally funded construction projects would bear the cost, through lower pay on government-financed jobs. Taxpayers might see some federal construction costs fall, but the reduction would come largely out of construction workers' wages.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would directly reduce pay for construction workers on federal projects, since prevailing-wage rules are the main mechanism guaranteeing government-funded construction pays local standard rates [S2].

The honest argument for repeal is that prevailing-wage requirements raise federal construction costs — the government often pays more for the same building than a private buyer would — so repeal could save taxpayer money on public works, though the savings come substantially out of workers' pay rather than pure efficiency.

The bill's nullification clause would strike prevailing-wage provisions embedded in many other federal laws at once, a broad rewrite of wage rules across programs with no new standards replacing them [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's one real benefit — lower bid prices on federal construction — would come mainly from paying workers less than the local standard. It offers no worker protections or training provisions in exchange, so the cost falls almost entirely on the people who build public projects. As written, it is a straightforward transfer of bargaining power from construction labor to contractors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on February 13, 2015, with six original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S3][S5].
Twelve Republicans cosponsored the bill, but the committee never acted on it, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 114th Congress [S4][S5].
The bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects are better off because prevailing-wage requirements remain in force. Contractors who wanted the option to pay below-market wages on federal jobs did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal construction workers, who kept wage rules

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to a committee vote during the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored, and the bill never got a vote where party breakdowns could be recorded [S4].

industries.note: Repeal would let contractors on federally funded projects pay below the locally prevailing wage, cutting their labor costs directly out of construction workers' pay. The public would see the same projects built with cheaper labor, and taxpayers would shoulder any savings only if contractors passed them along in bids.

industries.industry: Construction labor, especially unionized building trades
industries.note: Prevailing-wage rules effectively guarantee union-scale pay on federal construction; repeal would erase that floor and undercut union contractors bidding against lower-wage firms for public work.
Without prevailing-wage rules, smaller and nonunion firms would find it easier to compete for federal contracts. The same repeal lowers the wage floor their own employees would work under.
